summary: In Dynamic Range and Motion discussion, the photographer explains core perceptual differences between camera capture and human vision, emphasizing motion absence and limited dynamic range in still images. The talk contrasts complex rainforest scenes with simple arid landscapes to illustrate why two-dimensional media benefit from simplification and how motion aids depth perception. A central thread concerns dynamic range, with practical demonstrations that the useful shadow recovery on modern sensors typically spans roughly 1.6 to 3.1 stops, depending on the camera. The speaker details real-world testing across bodies (Nikon D850, Canon 5D III/IV, Sony, Fuji, etc.), the importance of precise highlight control, and how exposed-to-the-right thinking can help maximize shadow detail without excessive noise. He also covers post-processing strategies—sky removal, atmosphere introduction, painted light, and even sun/storm-light inserts from separate images—to craft painterly landscapes. The narration includes cautions about halo/artefact risk when blending exposures, the growing practicality of single-shot dynamic range with modern sensors, and panorama stitching (14-shot stitch) as a post-capture strategy. A concrete anecdote centers on a New Zealand shoot using a D850 at ISO 31 to illustrate low-noise, high-DR performance and the diminishing use of Graduated Neutral Density filters in light of sensor capabilities.

sections.title: Dynamic Range, Motion, and Post-Processing Principles in Landscape Photography
sections.description: A consolidated overview of how motion, dynamic range, and post-production choices shape landscape images. The presenter discusses how cameras lack motion and depth cues compared to the human eye, advocating simplification in complex scenes (e.g., rainforest) and the value of carefully controlling highlights to maximize useful shadow detail. The talk blends field strategy with detailed camera-based observations, including cross-brand comparisons, sensor performance assertions (3.1 stops as a practical DR limit in shadows), and the practical implications for printing. It also describes extensive post-processing workflows—sky removal, atmosphere creation, and light painting—along with techniques for assembling expansive scenes via stitching, all while warning against artefacts from exposure blending. The section weaves in explicit shooting anecdotes (e.g., a New Zealand shoot with a Nikon D850 at ISO 31) to ground theoretical claims in practice, and it contrasts science-backed limits with artistic endeavors (e.g., painterly light via post).
